Medication Interaction Reference for Post-Surgical Patients

This reference document describes known drug interactions relevant to patients recovering from orthopedic procedures. This document is intended for clinical reference and patient education. Always consult your pharmacist or physician before starting, stopping, or changing any medication.

Warfarin and Ibuprofen Interaction:
Severity: HIGH — Contraindicated combination in most post-surgical settings.
Description: Warfarin is an anticoagulant (blood thinner) commonly prescribed after joint replacement surgery to prevent deep vein thrombosis. Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). The combination of warfarin and ibuprofen significantly increases the risk of serious and potentially life-threatening bleeding events. Ibuprofen inhibits platelet aggregation and can irritate the gastric mucosa, both of which compound the anticoagulant effect of warfarin. Additionally, ibuprofen may displace warfarin from plasma protein binding sites, raising free warfarin levels and further elevating bleeding risk. Patients taking warfarin must avoid ibuprofen and all NSAIDs unless explicitly authorized by their prescribing physician. Source: medication-interaction-reference.

Warfarin and Aspirin Interaction:
Severity: MODERATE to HIGH — Use only when specifically prescribed and monitored.
Description: Aspirin also affects platelet function and can increase bleeding risk when combined with warfarin. Low-dose aspirin (81 mg/day) is sometimes prescribed alongside warfarin for specific cardiovascular indications under close medical supervision. Self-initiated aspirin use while on warfarin is not recommended without physician guidance. Regular INR monitoring is mandatory when these two agents are used together.

Warfarin and Naproxen Interaction:
Severity: HIGH — Same class as ibuprofen; avoid concurrent use.
Description: Naproxen, like ibuprofen, is an NSAID that inhibits platelet aggregation and can irritate the gastrointestinal tract. Its use alongside warfarin carries the same class-level risks as ibuprofen: significantly elevated bleeding risk, potential displacement of warfarin from protein-binding sites, and increased free warfarin concentration. Patients on warfarin should avoid naproxen unless specifically authorized.

Opioids and Benzodiazepines Interaction:
Severity: HIGH — Potentially fatal combination.
Description: Combining opioid pain medications (such as oxycodone or hydrocodone) with benzodiazepines (such as diazepam or alprazolam) carries a high risk of respiratory depression, sedation, and death. This combination should only be used under close medical supervision with careful dose management. Patients should inform all prescribers of their complete medication list.

Opioids and Alcohol Interaction:
Severity: HIGH — Contraindicated.
Description: Alcohol enhances the central nervous system depressant effects of opioid medications, increasing the risk of respiratory depression, sedation, overdose, and death. Patients taking opioid pain medications must abstain from alcohol during the course of opioid therapy.

Acetaminophen and Alcohol Interaction:
Severity: MODERATE — Avoid or strictly limit.
Description: Regular alcohol consumption while taking acetaminophen increases the risk of liver toxicity. Patients who consume 3 or more alcoholic beverages per day should not take acetaminophen without physician guidance.

Antibiotics and Warfarin Interaction:
Severity: MODERATE — Monitor INR closely.
Description: Many antibiotics, including fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) and metronidazole, can potentiate the anticoagulant effect of warfarin by reducing gut flora that produce vitamin K. Patients on warfarin who are prescribed antibiotics should have their INR monitored more frequently during and shortly after the antibiotic course.

Guidelines for Patients:
Always carry an up-to-date medication list. Inform every healthcare provider (including dentists and urgent care clinicians) of all medications you take. Do not start any new over-the-counter medication, supplement, or herbal product without first checking for interactions with your current prescriptions. If you are unsure whether two medications interact, contact your pharmacist — they are an accessible and expert resource for interaction checking.
